description.narrative: The Program Development Objectives is to strengthen the response to the COVID-19 pandemic, help protect the poor and most vulnerable, and lay the foundations for recovery by supporting SMEs and improving debt transparency.

The development objective COVID-19 Emergency Development Policy Operation is to strengthen the response to the Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, help protect the poor and most vulnerable, and lay the foundations for recovery by supporting Small and Medium Size Enterprises (SMEs) and improving debt transparency. This standalone operation aligns with the government's Coronavirus (COVID-19) response plan while contributing to close the financing gap. The operation is articulated around three mutually reinforcing pillars that balance the need to address critical emergency Coronavirus (COVID-19) related issues with putting in place elements of a medium-term framework for improving resilience: First pillar supports reforms to protect lives; Second Pillar supports reforms to protect livelihoods; and Third Pillar supports reforms to strengthen foundations for economic recovery.

title.narrative: Cumulative number of credit guarantees granted to SMEs by the Guarantee Fund

comment.narrative: <p><strong>The target for RI6 was not achieved. </strong>The number of credit guarantees extended to SMEs by the public credit guarantee (PCG) scheme was zero, not achieving the target to provide a cumulative 100 credit guarantees to SMEs by 2020 and by April 2022. Although the Government has prepared a detailed business plan, solicited private investment, signed a shareholders’ agreement, and secured interest from a fund manager for the PCG scheme for SMEs in 2019, the Government has not yet been able to provide public funding for it. Hence, it has not yet operationalized the fund. The Governor of the Central Bank explained that it continues toexplore options to secure some minimum public funding to operationalize the PCG scheme. He noted that the Ministry of Finance was unable to provide the capital required to operationalize the fund due to other priorities. However, the ICR team gathered from interviews with World Bank staff that there was no agreement between the Central Bank and Ministry of Finance regarding the entity that should head the Board of the PCG, leading to a misunderstanding that prevented the release of funds to the PCG. Unfortunately, the fund did not benefit from the FSSLCC, which has excess funds and below 50 percent of revenue execution as of February 2021. Assuming itbecomes operational in 2022, it will take some time for the PCG to extend 100 credit guarantees to SMEs as targeted. However, the pre-selected fund manager is top-notch in the region and globally, and, given the capacity constraints in the country and the intersectoral coordination needed, the Government may need to explore other country experience in the region to inform the implementation. For instance, in 2018, Burkina Faso set up an office in the Ministry of Finance, opened bank accounts in different regions, and administered the Support Fund for Women’s Income-Generating Activities (FAARF) though women’s associations and cooperative groups. These groups monitored their members and ensured the repayment of debts as it guaranteed higher loans for other members of their groups in subsequent years.</p>

title.narrative: Percent of expenditures of the Special Fund for Social Security and Fight Against Coronavirus devoted to COVID-19 mitigation measures audited by the Court of Accounts

comment.narrative:
<ol>
 <li><strong>The DPO target set for RI4 associated with prior action 3 was achieved by the end of 2020, and the reform could be sustained. </strong>The Court of Accounts audited 100 percent of expenditures (against a target for an audit of 90 percent) used from the FSSLCC devoted to COVID-19 mitigation by 2020. The audit report published in April 2022 covers expenditures from April 2020 to February 2021. It notes an execution of the fund’s revenue at 41.67 percent, indicating total expenditure of MRU 2.592 billion out of a total fund position of MRU 6.22 billion by February 2021. Of the audited expenditures, 84 percent of the funds were used for health expenditures, direct support to households, and tax expenditures. Compared to unaudited expenditures from the fund as of February 2022 (MRU 3.05 billion), 85 percent of the fund has been audited.[1] The Court of Accounts is empowered to continue regular audits of the fund by the organic law N° 2018-032 of July 20, 2018, relating to the Court of Accounts, the referral N°001/P/CFP of the President of the Public Finance Chamber of the Court of Accounts dated 05/01/2021 and decree N°066-2020 of 04/05/2020.</li>
</ol>

title.narrative: Share of households benefitting from the COVID-19 safety net response that has been identified from the Social Registry

comment.narrative:
<ol>
 <li><strong>The target set for RI5 was achieved and the reform is being sustained.</strong> As a result of the DPO, 83 percent of the 210,000 COVID-19 safety net response beneficiaries were drawn from the Social Registry, which had a roll of 174,016 households in February 2021<strong>.  </strong>RI5 was achieved and reflects the reliance on and use of the registry for the COVID-19 response. More importantly, this indicator also demonstrates progress toward the pillar objective of “Protecting Livelihoods,” which was concerned with ensuring the impact of COVID-19 was mitigated, particularly on the poorest and most vulnerable. Households in the registry are the poorest ones in Mauritania; targeting them ensures they are protected from the worst impacts of the crisis and falling into or deeper into poverty. The use of the registry to such a high degree (as evidenced by the high target) ensures it is a key tool that is mandated to be used by the Government. In addition, the targets were appropriate—the registry at the time of rollout did not cover all urban areas, though COVID-19 heavily affected urban areas. As such it was not possible to target 100 percent of beneficiaries using the registry. However, the registry did cover all rural areas where the majority of poor and vulnerable households are located. The target was exceeded since the share of households benefitting from the COVID-19 safety net response that were identified from the registry was 83 percent, exceeding the target of 75 percent. </li>
</ol>

title.narrative: Score on multilateral sector coordination following the One Health approach

comment.narrative:
<ol>
 <li><strong>The target set by the DPF for the result indicator 1 (RI1) associated with prior action 1 was Achieved. </strong>The score on multisectoral coordination following the One Health approach measures the extent to which the country is prepared to manage public health emergencies. In December 2020, the technical committee worked with an independent One Health committee to assess progress made, resulting in a score of 2 out of 5 levels. This is evidenced by an approved functional structure for organizing and responding to emerging diseases and logistics. The staff of the Ministry of Health shared “One Health Meeting Notes” indicating actions taken to address the outbreak of infectious diseases. The DPF targeted a score of 3, which indicates the Government had approved an action plan for regional collaboration and implemented a standard operating procedure to address a public health emergency. The result indicator is relevant, measurable, and appropriate given that it is applied uniformly across all countries involved in the One Health reforms to ensure comparability of reforms. The target is also reasonable given Mauritania did not have adequatesystems in place before the DPF. The target is considered to have been met with the existence of an Excel-based action plan indicating activities implemented through the budget in 2020 and 2021, plus proposed activities for 2022. However, the evidence is considered weak given that the action plan has not been published on the government website. Also, the Government missed the opportunity to have the action plan validated by an independent body in December 2021.</li>
</ol>

title.narrative: Percentage of the domestic debt of the general government, which is in the public domain

comment.narrative:
<p><strong>The target for RI7 was not achieved based on the stated DPO indicator, though the Government has improved the transparency of its debt reporting. </strong>The Government published two debt bulletins in December 2020 (covering the end of 2019 debt data)and December 2021 (covering 2020 debt data) as part of the Performance and Policy Actions in FY21 under the Sustainable DevelopmentFinance Policy. RI7 captures the deliberate decision of the Government to regularize BCM debt, which was included in the DSA but not previously reported as part of government debt. For the first time since 2018, the 2021 debt report recognized the conventional BCM debt of US$427 million, indicating progress toward debt transparency. To assess the achievement of the target, this evaluation assumes that domestic debt is accurately reported in the DSA Report for Mauritania by the World Bank and IMF, given it benefits from government debt reporting to both institutions. The Department of Finance External Debt Directorate <em>Statistical Bulletin on PublicDebt (2021)<strong>[1]</strong> </em>states that “local currency domestic debt is made up exclusively of short-term Treasury bills (traditional and Islamic bills) and represents 4.2 percent of outstanding public debt.” According to the report, outstanding Treasury bills were MRU 5.0 billion at the end of 2020, and outstanding Islamic Treasury bills were MRU 1.47 billion (Table 6).As these were all of Mauritania’s domestic debt at the end of 2020, then the Government was reporting 100 percent of its domestic debt. Compared to the domestic debt reported by the BCM (2020) and the July DSA of IMF, the debt bulletin of the Department of Finance External Debt Directorate continues to under-report the total domestic debt, reaching 28.5 percent below the target (90 percent), partly due to different definitions for domestic debt. The results are an improvement from equivalent data, which fell from 24.4 percent in 2019 to 22.1 percent in 2020. Based on the new domestic debt data published (including outstanding Islamic Treasury bills), the new baseline is 30.4 percent and outturn is 28.5 percent.</p>

<p> </p>

title.narrative: Average difference between the international price (CIF import price at port of terminal) and the domestic price (landed duty-paid price) for basic food products

comment.narrative:
<ol style="list-style-type:lower-alpha">
 <li>RI3 is achieved. The indicator sought to reduce the average difference between the international price (CIF import price at port of arrival) and domestic price (landed duty-paid price) for basic food products. Article3.2.4 listed the food items that had been exempted from the tariff in 2020. The results indicator covered exemptions on basic food items, such as milk powder, vegetable oil, soft wheat, and Semolina wheat, which were needed to protect lives during the COVID-19 pandemic.  These are products mostly consumed by a large segment of the population, including the poor. The average difference between the international price (CIF import price at port of arrival) and domestic price (landed duty-paid price) for basic food products was 6.2 percent against the target of 11 percent (Table 3). The budget law for 2021 (“Loi de Finances pour L’annee 2021”)[1] abolished the exemption on the listed basic food items, given that the pandemic was deemed reasonably under control at that time.   </li>
</ol>

<p> </p>

<p>[1] The abolition of the exoneration of food products is in the initial budget law 2021, page 13, article 3.2.4.</p>

title.narrative: Average difference between the international price (CIF import price at port of terminal) and the domestic price (landed duty-paid price) for COVID-19 medical products

comment.narrative:
<ol style="list-style-type:lower-alpha">
 <li>RI2 is achieved based on the methodology applied during the design of the operation. It was expected that the average difference between the international price of COVID-19 medical products (CIF import price at port of arrival) and the domestic price (landed duty paid price) would fall from a baseline of 29.0[1] percent in 2019 to a target of 13 percent as a result of the removal of tariffs. In 2020, the Government exempted the list of medical products for 9 months, indicatinga zero tariff for each of those products. The implementation of tariff exemptions was approved by the National Assembly[2] and the President as part of the 2020 supplementary budget. Article 3.2.5 listed the medical products exempted from the tariff. The average difference between the international price (CIF import price at port of arrival) and domestic price (landed duty-paid price) for COVID-19 medical products was 7.3 against the target of 13 percent (Annex 4). There was no evidence in the 2021 and 2022 budgets to indicate the removal of tariff exemptions on medical products.</li>
</ol>

<p> </p>

<p>[1] The ICR identified an error in the calculation of the baseline, which should be an average tariff rate of 29 percent instead of 29.4 percent in the program document. The methodology for calculating the average tariff was demonstrated to the ICR team by the Government but tagged confidential.</p>

<p>[2] Pages 28–30 in articles 3.2.4 and 3.2.5 for the supplementary budget law no. 2020-006 rectified for 2020.</p>
